claim: Both passive exposure and active learning through reinforcement enhance fine sensory discrimination abilities.
source: Both passive exposure and active learning through reinforcement enhance fine sensory discrimination abilities.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: Enhancement of fine sensory discrimination in the olfactory system is thought to occur partially through the integration of adult-born inhibitory interneurons.
source: In the olfactory system, this enhancement is thought to occur partially through the integration of adult-born inhibitory interneurons resulting in a refinement of the representation of overlapping odorants.
evidence: This is presented as current understanding in the field.

claim: Integration of adult-born inhibitory interneurons results in a refinement of the representation of overlapping odorants.
source: In the olfactory system, this enhancement is thought to occur partially through the integration of adult-born inhibitory interneurons resulting in a refinement of the representation of overlapping odorants.
evidence: This is presented as current understanding in the field.

claim: Both passive and active learning processes augment neurogenesis in mice.
source: Specifically, while both passive and active learning processes augment neurogenesis, adult-born cells differ in their morphology, functional coupling and thus their impact on olfactory bulb output.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Adult-born cells differ in their morphology between passive and active learning.
source: Specifically, while both passive and active learning processes augment neurogenesis, adult-born cells differ in their morphology, functional coupling and thus their impact on olfactory bulb output.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by morphological analysis data in the results.

claim: Adult-born cells differ in their functional coupling between passive and active learning.
source: Specifically, while both passive and active learning processes augment neurogenesis, adult-born cells differ in their morphology, functional coupling and thus their impact on olfactory bulb output.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiological data in the results.

claim: Adult-born cells differ in their impact on olfactory bulb output between passive and active learning.
source: Specifically, while both passive and active learning processes augment neurogenesis, adult-born cells differ in their morphology, functional coupling and thus their impact on olfactory bulb output.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mitral cell recording data in the results.

claim: Passive learning induces increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons.
source: Morphological analysis, optogenetic stimulation of adult-born neurons and mitral cell recordings revealed that passive learning induces increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons, probably resulting in more sparse and thus less overlapping odor representations.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis, optogenetic stimulation, and mitral cell recordings presented in the results.

claim: Increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons after passive learning probably results in more sparse odor representations.
source: Morphological analysis, optogenetic stimulation of adult-born neurons and mitral cell recordings revealed that passive learning induces increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons, probably resulting in more sparse and thus less overlapping odor representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased inhibition and decreased mitral cell activation.

claim: Increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons after passive learning probably results in less overlapping odor representations.
source: Morphological analysis, optogenetic stimulation of adult-born neurons and mitral cell recordings revealed that passive learning induces increased inhibitory action by adult-born neurons, probably resulting in more sparse and thus less overlapping odor representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased inhibition and decreased mitral cell activation.

claim: After active learning, inhibitory action by adult-born neurons is diminished due to reduced connectivity.
source: Conversely, after active learning inhibitory action is found to be diminished due to reduced connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing reduced spine density and electrophysiological data showing reduced inhibition.

claim: Strengthened odor response might underlie enhanced discriminability after active learning.
source: In this case, strengthened odor response might underlie enhanced discriminability.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed increased mitral cell responsiveness after active learning.

claim: Adult neurogenesis is a plasticity mechanism mediating changes in representations of sensory information.
source: Several lines of evidence suggested that adult neurogenesis is a plasticity mechanism mediating changes in representations of sensory information (Lledo and Valley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Experience-dependent survival of adult-born neurons is a mechanism to modulate pattern separation and perceptual discrimination in the hippocampus and olfactory bulb.
source: Experience-dependent survival of adult-born neurons has received recent attention as a mechanism to modulate pattern separation and perceptual discrimination in the hippocampus and olfactory bulb (OB) (Sahay et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Current hypotheses about the mechanism underlying enhanced discrimination capability in the OB focus on increased inhibitory processes mediated by GABAergic adult-born neurons.
source: In the OB, current hypotheses about the mechanism underlying this enhanced discrimination capability focus on increased inhibitory processes mediated by GABAergic adult-born neurons (Moreno et al., 2009; Alonso et al., 2012), with more integrating cells delivering more inhibition, leading to sparser odor representations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The current hypothesis proposes that more integrating cells deliver more inhibition, leading to sparser odor representations.
source: In the OB, current hypotheses about the mechanism underlying this enhanced discrimination capability focus on increased inhibitory processes mediated by GABAergic adult-born neurons (Moreno et al., 2009; Alonso et al., 2012), with more integrating cells delivering more inhibition, leading to sparser odor representations.
evidence: This is the current hypothesis in the field as indicated by citations.

claim: The data presented challenge the current hypothesis by showing that the same rate of adult-born cell survival in the OB can enhance fine olfactory discrimination by either increasing or decreasing OB output sparseness.
source: The data presented here challenge the current hypothesis by showing that the same rate of adult-born cell survival in the OB can enhance fine olfactory discrimination by either increasing or decreasing OB output sparseness.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Both passive (implicit perceptual learning in response to repeated exposure) and active (explicit associative learning in response to reinforcement) learning can improve discrimination between similar odorants in the olfactory system.
source: In the olfactory system, both passive (implicit perceptual learning in response to repeated exposure) and active (explicit associative learning in response to reinforcement) learning can improve discrimination between similar odorants (Mandairon et al., 2006a; Moreno et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both forms of learning have been shown to modulate neural activity in the OB.
source: Both forms of learning have been shown to modulate neural activity in the OB (Buonviso et al., 1998; Kay and Laurent, 1999; Doucette et al., 2011), and to increase survival of inhibitory adult-born interneurons (Moreno et al., 2009; Sultan et al., 2010; Mandairon et al., 2011; Sultan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both forms of learning increase survival of inhibitory adult-born interneurons.
source: Both forms of learning have been shown to modulate neural activity in the OB (Buonviso et al., 1998; Kay and Laurent, 1999; Doucette et al., 2011), and to increase survival of inhibitory adult-born interneurons (Moreno et al., 2009; Sultan et al., 2010; Mandairon et al., 2011; Sultan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: +limonene and -limonene are not spontaneously discriminated by mice.
source: To induce implicit learning, animals were exposed to two odorants, which are not spontaneously discriminated: +limonene (+lim) and - limonene (-lim).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the experimental design and is supported by behavioral data in controls.

claim: Enriched animals discriminated +lim and -lim at the end of the enrichment procedure as evidenced by increased investigation times between the last habituation trial and the test trial (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.004).
source: Enriched animals discriminated +lim and -lim at the end of the enrichment procedure as evidenced by increased investigation times between the last habituation trial (OHab4) and the test trial (OTest) (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.004) whereas the controls did not (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.74) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Control non-enriched animals did not discriminate +lim and -lim (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.74).
source: Enriched animals discriminated +lim and -lim at the end of the enrichment procedure as evidenced by increased investigation times between the last habituation trial (OHab4) and the test trial (OTest) (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.004) whereas the controls did not (Wilcoxon test for discrimination p=0.74) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Implicit learning increased adult-born granule cell survival (p=0.042, parametric Anova followed by Bonferroni post hoc test).
source: As expected, implicit learning increased adult-born granule cell survival (p=0.042, parametric Anova followed by Bonferroni post hoc test; Non-Enriched n = 6 and Enriched n = 4, see methods for global statistics strategy), (Table 1; Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by BrdU quantification data shown in Figure 1C and Table 1.

claim: Implicit learning increased adult-born granule cell responsiveness to the learned odors as assessed by BrdU/Zif268 co-expression (p=0.0078, parametric Anova followed by Bonferroni post hoc tests).
source: As expected, implicit learning increased adult-born granule cell survival (p=0.042, parametric Anova followed by Bonferroni post hoc test; Non-Enriched n = 6 and Enriched n = 4, see methods for global statistics strategy), (Table 1; Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) as well as their responsiveness to the learned odors as assessed by BrdU/Zif268 co-expression (p=0.0078, parametric Anova followed by Bonferroni post hoc tests; Non-Enriched n = 7 and Enriched n = 6), (Table 1; Figure 1D and Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Moreno et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 1D and Table 1.

claim: Spine density increased after implicit learning on the apical dendrites of adult-born granule cells (p=0.0003, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation tests).
source: Spine density increased after implicit learning on both the apical (p=0.0003, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation tests; Non-Enriched: 48 segments, four mice and Enriched: 30 segments, four mice) (Table 1; Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: Spine density increased after implicit learning on the basal dendritic domains of adult-born granule cells (p=0.0015, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation tests).
source: and basal dendritic domains (p=0.0015, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation tests; Non-Enriched: 59 segments, seven mice and Enriched: 48 segments, seven mice), (Table 1; Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 1G and Table 1.

claim: 5 to 6 weeks after enrichment, once the enriched animals had forgotten the task, the density of BrdU-positive cells had returned to control values.
source: In addition, 5 to 6 weeks after enrichment, once the enriched animals had forgotten the task, the density of BrdU-positive cells and the spine density on adult-born cells had returned to control values (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 5 to 6 weeks after enrichment, once the enriched animals had forgotten the task, the spine density on adult-born cells had returned to control values.
source: In addition, 5 to 6 weeks after enrichment, once the enriched animals had forgotten the task, the density of BrdU-positive cells and the spine density on adult-born cells had returned to control values (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current (sIPSC) frequency recorded on M/T cells showed a trend toward increase after implicit learning (p=0.06).
source: Spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current (sIPSC) frequency recorded on M/T cells showed a trend toward increase after implicit learning (p=0.06, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test, Enriched, n = 50 and Non-Enriched, n = 48) (for detailed statistics see Table 1), (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1) with no change in amplitude (Table 1, Enriched n = 48 and Non-Enriched, n = 46).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1H and Table 1.

claim: There was no change in sIPSC amplitude after implicit learning.
source: Spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current (sIPSC) frequency recorded on M/T cells showed a trend toward increase after implicit learning (p=0.06, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test, Enriched, n = 50 and Non-Enriched, n = 48) (for detailed statistics see Table 1), (Figure 1H and Figure 1—source data 1) with no change in amplitude (Table 1, Enriched n = 48 and Non-Enriched, n = 46).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Table 1.

claim: Light stimulation of adult-born granule cells had an overall effect on M/T cells eIPSC frequency (light effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.37, p=0.037).
source: Data analysis indicated an overall effect of light stimulation of granule cells on M/T cells eIPSC frequency (light effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.37, p=0.037, paired t-tests for light versus pre light: p=0.0025 in the enriched group, p=0.2 in the non-enriched group) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: eIPSC frequency was higher in enriched compared to Non-enriched animals (learning effect, parametric ANOVA, F(1,198)=4.47, p=0.03).
source: Besides, eIPSC frequency was higher in enriched compared to Non-enriched animals (learning effect, parametric ANOVA, F(1,198)=4.47, p=0.03, t-test for difference between Enriched and non-enriched under light stimulation, p=0.04) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: No change in eIPSC amplitude was observed after implicit learning.
source: No change in eIPSC amplitude was observed (parametric ANOVA, light effect F(1,160)=2.66, p=0.1, learning effect F(1,160)=1.72, p=0.19) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The percentage of light-responding M/T cells is marginally increased in enriched compared to non-enriched animals (unilateral Chi squared, p=0.07).
source: Results indicated that the percentage of light-responding M/T cells is marginally increased in enriched compared to non-enriched animals (unilateral Chi squared, p=0.07; Figure 1I right and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The biophysical properties of adult-born granule cells (resting potential, membrane resistance, membrane capacitance and input/output curves) were unaffected by implicit learning.
source: Additionally, we showed that the biophysical properties of adult-born granule cells (resting potential, membrane resistance, membrane capacitance and input/output curves) were unaffected by learning (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Increased structural and/or functional connectivity is responsible for increased granule-to-M/T cell inhibition in enriched versus non-enriched groups, rather than any modification of the intrinsic properties of adult-born granule cells.
source: Thus, the results from these experiments suggest that increased structural and/or functional connectivity is responsible for increased granule-to-M/T cell inhibition in enriched versus non-enriched groups, rather than any modification of the intrinsic properties of adult-born granule cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined morphological and electrophysiological data.

claim: Implicit learning decreased the number of odor-activated M/T cells compared to non-enriched controls (Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.02).
source: We found that implicit learning decreased the number of odor-activated M/T cells compared to non-enriched controls (587 ± 29 M/T cells counted per animal; Enr, n = 5 and Non-Enr, n = 4; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.02; Table 1, Figure 1J and Figure 1—source data 1), resulting in a sparser representation of learned odorants at the OB output.
evidence: This is supported by Tbx21/Zif268 co-expression data shown in Figure 1J and Table 1.

claim: Implicit learning results in a sparser representation of learned odorants at the OB output.
source: We found that implicit learning decreased the number of odor-activated M/T cells compared to non-enriched controls (587 ± 29 M/T cells counted per animal; Enr, n = 5 and Non-Enr, n = 4; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.02; Table 1, Figure 1J and Figure 1—source data 1), resulting in a sparser representation of learned odorants at the OB output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decreased number of odor-activated M/T cells.

claim: The finding of sparser M/T odor responses is highly consistent with the increased inhibition of M/T cells observed in slice recordings.
source: This finding is highly consistent with the increased inhibition of M/T cells observed in slice recordings.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the in vivo and in vitro findings.

claim: In the context of implicit learning, adult-born granule cells provide more inhibitory contacts on M/T cells, leading to increased sparseness of M/T odor responses.
source: Altogether, in the context of implicit learning, adult-born granule cells provide more inhibitory contacts on M/T cells, leading to increased sparseness of M/T odor responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined experimental data.

claim: A decreased overlap between learned odor representations mediates the observed increase in odor discrimination after implicit learning.
source: As a consequence, these findings strongly support the hypothesis that a decreased overlap between learned odor representations mediates the observed increase in odor discrimination (Chu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: Discrimination could be achieved through increasing the resolution of the odor representations.
source: Theoretically, discrimination could also be achieved through increasing the resolution of the odor representations (Aimone et al., 2011), in other words through increasing the response to the learned odorant (Doucette and Restrepo, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility supported by citations.

claim: Adding information to the representation of the stimulus could ultimately help discrimination.
source: Indeed, adding information to the representation of the stimulus could ultimately help discrimination, and we hypothesized that such a mechanism could be involved in associative learning where the odor is reinforced by a positive reward.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Training in the conditioned group was evidenced by an increase of correct choices (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.03).
source: Training took place over 5 days (four trials/day) and was evidenced by an increase of correct choices in the conditioned (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.03) but not in the pseudo-conditioned group (PC) (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.57; Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No increase in correct choices was observed in the pseudo-conditioned group (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.57).
source: Training took place over 5 days (four trials/day) and was evidenced by an increase of correct choices in the conditioned (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.03) but not in the pseudo-conditioned group (PC) (n = 20; Friedman test day effect p=0.57; Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Conditioned but not pseudo-conditioned animals discriminated +lim from –lim as confirmed by habituation/cross habituation test.
source: Using the habituation/cross habituation test, we confirmed that conditioned but not pseudo-conditioned animals discriminated +lim from –lim as they did with implicit learning (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Explicit learning induced an increase in the survival of adult-born granule cells (n = 6/group; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.025).
source: As with implicit learning, explicit learning induced an increase in the survival of adult-born granule cells (n = 6/group; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.025; Table 1; Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by BrdU quantification data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Explicit learning induced an increase in adult-born granule cell responsiveness to the learned odor (+lim), as assessed by BrdU/Zif268 co-expression (n = 7/group; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.005).
source: as well as an increase in their responsiveness to the learned odor (+lim), as assessed by BrdU/Zif268 co-expression (n = 7/group; Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.005; Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: In contrast to implicit learning, explicit learning showed a decrease in spine density on the apical dendrites after conditioning compared to pseudo-conditioning (non-parametric corrected test p=0.0025).
source: However, in contrast to implicit learning, analysis of the fine morphology of adult-born neuron dendrites showed a decrease in spine density on the apical dendrites after conditioning compared to pseudo-conditioning (Cond 106 segments, four mice and PC 56 segments, five mice; non-parametric corrected test p=0.0025; Figure 2E and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: No change in spine density was observed in the basal domain after explicit learning (non-parametric corrected test p=0.09).
source: while no such change was observed in the basal domain (Cond: 37 segments, four mice and PC: 43 segments, four mice; non-parametric corrected test p=0.09; Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2F and Table 1.

claim: 42 days after conditioning, when discrimination had returned to control levels, the spine density had also returned to control values.
source: 42 days after conditioning, when discrimination had returned to control levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), the spine density had also returned to control values (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The morphological changes of adult-born neurons paralleled discrimination performance.
source: This indicated that the morphological changes of adult-born neurons paralleled discrimination performance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation between spine density and discrimination ability.

claim: sIPSCs amplitude was decreased after explicit learning (p=0.015, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test).
source: We further analyzed the impact of adult-born neurons on M/T cell activity by recording sIPSCs from M/T cells in OB slices. sIPSCs amplitude was decreased (p=0.015, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test; Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: sIPSCs frequency was marginally affected after explicit learning (p=0.06, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test).
source: while their frequency was marginally affected (p=0.06, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test; Table 1) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: The sIPSC data suggest a global reduction of M/T cell inhibition in the OB in conditioned versus pseudo-conditioned animals.
source: sIPSCs amplitude was decreased (p=0.015, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test; Table 1) while their frequency was marginally affected (p=0.06, Kruskal-Wallis Anova followed by FDR-corrected permutation test; Table 1) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—source data 1) suggesting a global reduction of M/T cell inhibition in the OB in conditioned versus pseudo-conditioned animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data.

claim: Light stimulation of adult-born granule cells induced an increase in M/T cell eIPSC frequency in both conditioned and pseudo-conditioned animals compared to pre-light (light effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.37, p=0.037).
source: The light stimulation of adult-born granule cells induced an increase in M/T cell eIPSC frequency in both conditioned and pseudo-conditioned animals compared to pre-light (light effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.37, p=0.037, paired t-tests for light versus pre light, p=0.015 in the pseudo-conditioned group, n = 46 cells from five mice; p=0.001 in the conditioned group, n = 34 cells from three mice) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: eIPSC frequency was lower in conditioned compared to pseudo-conditioned animals (learning effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.47, p=0.03).
source: Besides, eIPSC frequency was lower in conditioned compared to pseudo-conditioned animals (learning effect, parametric Anova, F(1,198)=4.47, p=0.03, t-test for difference between conditioned and pseudo-conditioned groups under light stimulation, p=0.0015; Pseudo-conditioned n = 22 cells from two mice; Conditioned n = 28 cells from two mice) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The percentage of M/T cells responding to light stimulation of adult-born granule cells by an increased eIPSC frequency was lower in conditioning compared to pseudo-conditioning (Unilateral Chi squared test, p=0.007).
source: Analysis of individual cell responses showed the percentage of M/T cells responding to light stimulation of adult-born granule cells by an increased eIPSC frequency was lower in conditioning compared to pseudo-conditioning (Unilateral Chi squared test, p=0.007), (Figure 2H and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The biophysical properties of adult-born granule cells (resting potential, membrane resistance, membrane capacitance and input/output curves) were not affected by explicit learning.
source: The biophysical properties of adult-born granule cells (resting potential, membrane resistance, membrane capacitance and input/output curves) were not affected by explicit learning (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inhibitory inputs to M/T cells were decreased after explicit learning.
source: As a consequence, we concluded that inhibitory inputs to M/T cells were decreased after explicit learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electrophysiological data.

claim: Explicit learning showed a significant increase in mitral cell responsiveness to the learned odor (Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.04).
source: The functional outcome of this decreased inhibition was assessed using Tbx21/Zif268 co-expression in mitral cells (540 ± 20 mitral cells counted per animal; n = 5 animals/group), and showed a significant increase in mitral cell responsiveness to the learned odor, (Bonferroni-corrected test p=0.04; Figure 2I and Figure 2—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by Tbx21/Zif268 co-expression data shown in Figure 2I and Table 1.

claim: After explicit learning, odor representations at the OB output were not rendered sparser.
source: suggesting that in this case, odor representations at the OB output were not rendered sparser by learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased mitral cell responsiveness.

claim: Explicit and implicit learnings similarly increased adult-born survival (learning versus controls F(1,18)=19.72, p=0.0003), regardless of the type of learning (implicit versus explicit F(1, 18)=0.21, p=0.64).
source: Using a two-factor Anova, we found that explicit and implicit learnings similarly increased adult-born survival (learning versus controls F(1,18)=19.72, p=0.0003), regardless of the type of learning (implicit versus explicit F(1, 18)=0.21, p=0.64 and no interaction F(1,18)=0.006, p 0.9) (Figure 1C and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of BrdU data across learning types.

claim: Both learning types similarly increased adult-born cells responsiveness to the learned odor (learning effect F(1,23)=27.70, p<0.0001, no effect of the type of learning F(1, 23)=0.23, p=0.87).
source: The same was true for adult-born cells responsiveness to the learned odor (learning effect F(1,23)=27.70, p<0.0001, no effect of the type of learning F(1, 23)=0.23, p=0.87, no interaction F(1,23)=0.0001, p=0.98) (Figure 1D and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of BrdU/Zif268 data across learning types.

claim: Implicit learning resulted in stronger inhibition on M/T cells than did explicit learning as shown by lower sIPSC amplitude in conditioned versus enriched groups (p=0.0048, FDR-corrected permutation test).
source: However, implicit learning resulted in stronger inhibition on M/T cells than did explicit learning as shown by lower sIPSC amplitude in conditioned versus enriched groups (p=0.0048, FDR-corrected permutation test, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of sIPSC data between learning types.

claim: Adult-born granule cells bear more spines in enriched compared to conditioned groups in their apical domain which interacts with mitral cells (p=0.0003, FDR-corrected permutation test).
source: In addition, adult-born granule cells bear more spines in enriched compared to conditioned groups in their apical domain which interacts with mitral cells (p=0.0003, FDR-corrected permutation test, Table 1, Figure 1F,G; Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of spine density data between learning types.

claim: M/T cells displayed lower responsiveness to the learned odorant in enriched compared to conditioned animals (p=0.015, Bonferroni post hoc test).
source: In line with this, M/T cells displayed lower responsiveness to the learned odorant in enriched compared to conditioned animals (p=0.015, Bonferroni post hoc test, Tbx21/Zif268, Table 1, Figure 1J and Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of Tbx21/Zif268 data between learning types.

claim: sIPSC frequencies were higher in the pseudo-conditioned compared to the non-enriched animals (p=0.0006, FDR-corrected permutation test).
source: Interestingly, when comparing the controls for each learning group (pseudo-conditioned versus non-enriched) (Table 1), they appeared to differ. More precisely, sIPSC frequencies were higher in the pseudo-conditioned compared to the non-enriched animals (p=0.0006, FDR-corrected permutation test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of control groups.

claim: The number of odor-activated M/T cells tended to be smaller in the pseudo-conditioned than the non-enriched animals (p=0.053 Bonferroni post hoc test).
source: Consistent with this, the number of odor-activated M/T cells tended to be smaller in the pseudo-conditioned than the non-enriched animals (p=0.053 Bonferroni post hoc test, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of control groups.

claim: The differences between pseudo-conditioned and non-enriched animals could be explained by the fact that the pseudo-conditioned animals, in contrast to the non-enriched animals were exposed to the odorants throughout the pseudo-conditioning procedure.
source: These differences could be explained by the fact that the pseudo-conditioned animals, in contrast to the non-enriched animals were exposed to the odorants throughout the pseudo-conditioning procedure.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differences between control groups.

claim: The pseudo-conditioned animals shared cellular similarities with enriched animals (similar sIPSC frequency, percentage of odor-activated M/T cells and basal spine density) despite the fact that they do not show behavioral discrimination.
source: Finally, we observed that the pseudo-conditioned animals shared cellular similarities with enriched animals (similar sIPSC frequency, percentage of odor-activated M/T cells and basal spine density) (Table 1) despite the fact that they do not show behavioral discrimination.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of multiple measures across groups.

claim: Implicit learning increased spine density on adult-born granule cells (apical and basal dendritic domains), in agreement with previous studies.
source: Implicit learning increased spine density on adult-born granule cells (apical and basal dendritic domains), in agreement with previous studies (Daroles et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: This finding is supported by the current data and citations to previous work.
